newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: WFP rushes food convoys to Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: WFP rushes food convoys to Afghanistan.

text.p: The U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) said on Friday it had rushed food convoys to war-shattered Afghanistan where supplies had been badly hit by a Pakistani border closure.

An extra 16-truck convoy with 250 tonnes of wheat flour will reach the Afghan capital Kabul on Saturday after the arrival of 16-truck convoy with 300 tonnes of wheat on Wednesday and a 23-truck convoy with 605 tonnes of wheat on March 28, a WFP statement in Islamabad said.
"This move has been made in response to the current shortage of wheat flour and the resulting escalation in price inside Afghanistan," it said.

"We are tracking the situation on a daily basis," it quoted WFP country director for Afghanistan Anis Haider as saying. "The WFP warehouses in Kabul are full, with almost 7,000 tonnes of wheat or wheat flour in stock," he added.
Pakistan sealed its border on March 27 to check wheat smuggling out of the country to meet shortages of wheat flour.
Pakistan's border closure on account of its wheat shortages "has seriously affected food supply to Afghanistan as a whole and especially to the capital", the WFP statement said.
The WFP said while food was still available in Kabul, the wheat flour price as of April 2 was 10,400 afghanis per kilo, up from 6,800 two weeks ago and almost twice as much in February.

"In addition to the escalation in price due to the border closure, early spring is traditionally a time of hardship in Afghanistan, a lean time to be endured while waiting for the first wheat harvest to become available," the statement said.
It cited an influx of displaced people from northern front lines as another reason for food price rises in Kabul, where it said more than 140,000 people had sought refuge since October.

To help meet these difficult times, the WFP has extended for two more months its bakery project that provides highly subsidised bread to almost 210,000 of the poorest Kabulis, including widows, households headed by women, the displaced, the elderly, the unemployed, the disabled and orphans, it said.
It said the flour shortage was also affecting other communities in Afghanistan such as those in Jalalabad and Kandahar regions in the east and south respectivly.
"There, too, the prices of basic food are rising, and WFP bakeries reach out to almost a quarter of a million of the most needy." it said.

In western Afghanistan, WFP is providing emergency food aid to amost 3,000 victims of recent floods in 18 villages that destroyed homes, dikes, canals, culverts and fields and washed out part of the vital Herat-Torghundi road, it said.
